edges.description: CSD releases inflammatory mediators (HMGB1, prostaglandins) via pannexin-1 channels and activates meningeal trigeminal nociceptors, driving the trigeminovascular activation that initiates the headache phase.
Activated trigeminal afferents release PACAP alongside CGRP, so trigeminovascular activation feeds the PACAP arm as well as the CGRP one.
Activated trigeminal afferents release CGRP from peripheral nerve and central nerve terminals, initiating vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation in the meninges.

Trigeminovascular activation during an attack reaches structures anatomically and functionally linked to the vestibular system, not only the pain pathways, which is the upstream entry point for the vestibular arm of this entry.

Peripheral CGRP release perpetuates trigeminal nerve sensitization and drives central sensitization of second-order neurons in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis and thalamus, producing allodynia and enhanced pain perception.

CGRP released during the attack acts on trigeminal terminals innervating inner ear structures and on CGRP receptors in the vestibular nuclei, so the same peptide that drives the pain arm also drives the vestibular one.

Sensitized vestibular nuclei drive abnormal activity and altered multisensory integration in the vestibulo-thalamo-cortical networks, causing impaired balance between vestibular, visual, and auditory inputs. This produces motion intolerance, visual motion sensitivity, and vertigo.

Abnormal vestibulo-thalamo-cortical integration produces vestibular symptoms (spontaneous, positional, visually-induced, or head-motion-induced vertigo/dizziness) that may occur with or without headache during vestibular migraine attacks.

Failure of cerebellar canal-otolith synthesis contributes to the vestibular symptoms of an attack through the same convergence sites at which trigeminal and vestibular signals interact. Reversibility of this arm is what vestibular rehabilitation is thought to exploit.

CGRP released from activated trigeminal terminals drives sensitization of vestibular nuclei through peripheral and central mechanisms, amplifying trigemino-vestibular interactions and central vestibular dysfunction.
PACAP released during the headache phase contributes to nociceptive transmission within the trigeminovascular system, alongside CGRP, and so feeds the sensitization that maintains the attack.
Caffeine withdrawal and monosodium glutamate provoke migraine attacks in controlled provocation studies.

nodes.description: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide (PACAP) is expressed in migraine-related regions including the hypothalamus, pons, thalamus, trigeminal ganglia and trigeminal nucleus caudalis, and operates at least partly in parallel to CGRP in trigeminovascular nociceptive signaling. PACAP infusion provokes migraine attacks in susceptible individuals, and the pathway is a target for preventive therapy.

nodes.description: Glutamatergic projections from the caudal trigeminal nucleus directly innervate vestibular nuclei. During migraine attacks, trigeminal nociceptive activation and CGRP release from trigeminal terminals drive vestibular nucleus sensitization, generating central vestibular hypersensitivity. This pathway is the mechanistic bridge linking migraine biology to vestibular symptoms in vestibular migraine.

evidence.reference_title: Vestibular Migraine: A Systematic Literature Search and Narrative Review of Diagnostic Criteria, Pathophysiology, Differential Diagnosis, and Treatment Approaches.
evidence.snippet: The trigemino-vestibular projection is glutamatergic, originates in the caudal trigeminal nucleus, and projects to the vestibular nuclei, where it mediates vestibular dysfunction in chronic nitroglycerin migraine models; silencing this projection reduces vestibular dysfunction.

evidence.reference_title: Vestibular Migraine: A Systematic Literature Search and Narrative Review of Diagnostic Criteria, Pathophysiology, Differential Diagnosis, and Treatment Approaches.
evidence.snippet: Trigeminal nociceptive pathways interact with vestibular nuclei, which generate central sensitivity during attacks. Experimental models demonstrate both glutamatergic projections from the caudal trigeminal nucleus to the vestibular nuclei and increased neuronal activation in vestibular centers following migraine provocation.

evidence.reference_title: Vestibular Migraine: A Systematic Literature Search and Narrative Review of Diagnostic Criteria, Pathophysiology, Differential Diagnosis, and Treatment Approaches.
evidence.snippet: Following chronic migraine paradigms, abnormal synaptic protein expression and altered synaptic morphology have been reported in the vestibular nucleus, consistent with central sensitization processes.

evidence.snippet: Evidence suggests that attacks are primarily caused by abnormal central processing and integration of vestibular, visual, and nociceptive inputs, rather than by entirely peripheral labyrinthine insufficiency. Studies have identified impairments in canal-otolith integration, alterations in vestibulo-ocular responses, and dysfunction in the vestibulo-thalamocortical and cerebellar networks that process multisensory vestibular signals.

Phenotypes associated with widespread cutaneous allodynia, sleep disturbances, tinnitus, depressive symptoms, and high disability can be interpreted as clinical manifestations of increased sensitivity in thalamocortical sensory processing.

nodes.description: CGRP is expressed in trigeminal terminals innervating the inner ear, vestibular nuclei, and vestibulo-cerebellar networks. CGRP release during migraine attacks increases excitability and sensitivity in central vestibular pathways (via PKC/ERK/CREB activation) and modulates peripheral inner ear electrophysiology. This dual-level CGRP signaling (peripheral and central) is the mechanistic basis for CGRP-targeted therapy efficacy in vestibular migraine.

nodes.description: The vestibulocerebellum and deep cerebellar nuclei are among the sites where vestibular and trigeminal nociceptive signals converge, and they carry the canal-otolith integration that builds a stable percept of head orientation. Defective central synthesis of cerebellar origin is inferred from raised thresholds and delayed tilt perception under combined canal-otolith stimulation. The same networks are the substrate for recovery: cerebellar functional activity changes after vestibular rehabilitation, which is why this node carries both the deficit and the compensation it permits. This is the fifth of the five mechanism families the source's own summary names, and it is the one that makes vestibular rehabilitation mechanistically intelligible rather than merely empirical.

Central sensitization of thalamocortical networks produces widespread sensory hypersensitivity (allodynia, tinnitus, visual/auditory oversensitivity).
